utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Due to unfortunate and unforeseen circumstances, Judge Fluegge is not with us this morning. Travelling, he met some obstacles. That's the reason why he's not back. We expect him to be back tomorrow. For this reason, we'll continue to sit Rule 15 bis as we had decided to do last Friday, Judge Fluegge being unable. Judge Moloto and I considered it in the interests of justice to continue to hear the case. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time for a few short matters or at least one. The first one deals with a map which was introduced through Witness Jevdjevic. It's D909. During the testimony of that witness a map was marketed by the witness, uploaded into e-court, and then admitted into evidence as Exhibit D909. The Chamber hereby clarifies that the actual map as opposed to the scanned copy forms part of the exhibit and accordingly the Registry should retain custody over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pelemis, before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. McCloskey will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before the weekend, my colleague, Mr. Lukic, pointed out a mistake I had made in a question. I want to clear that up for you and for us. At page 33796, I asked you: "Well, you know Erdemovic testified that you issued the orders for them to go kill people so -- and you weren't interested?" And you answered: "I never issued that order to Erdemovic." And in that question, that was not completely correct. Let me clear that up and read to you what Erdemovic has actually testified to so you're not misled. And on page 13756 of his testimony in this case, he said, line 6: "As I've said already, Brano Gojkovic came to our rooms where we slept and he told me and Franc Kos and Zoran Gorenje to get ready, that we were going on a mission, that Pelemis had ordered it." And he went to say that at the Branjevo farm he received orders to kill from Brano Gojkovic. So -- but I do want you to know that it is our position that the mission that Erdemovic says you ordered through Gojkovic, it's our position that when you did issue that order, you knew that it was an issue -- an order to kill people. And I take it you still deny that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I again deny that I could have issued that order, especially since we are talking about Brano Gojkovic, a private who has no authority to command Erdemovic and Franc. Even if I had been there, certainly that sequence of issuing orders would not have been right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing that was asked, whether you do deny that you gave such an order. Whether you could have done it or whether it should have been done, that's a different question. Please stick very much to the question as put to you by Mr. McCloskey. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it if you say, "I couldn't have given that order," that you actually want to say, "I did not give that order." Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you also had challenged the number of victims at the Branjevo farm, and I wanted to try to clear that up. At P01 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't believe we need to put this on e-court, it's very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At P01673, the testimony at the hearing, Rule 61, in 1996, Erdemovic said that: "On the 16th sometime about 1 -- somewhere about 1200, I do not know. I estimate that the number according to the arrivals of the buses, civilians killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to P01987. It should be e-court page 41 and page 45 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a report -- from a report by an investigator named Dusan Janc who has assembled all the numbers of people taken out of the graves at Branjevo farm and those that had been forensically connected to secondary graves from Branjevo farm. And after this many years, many -- many, if not all, the graves associated with Branjevo farm have been exhumed, and by DNA analysis individuals have been identified and counted. And we can see from this report - e-court page 41 in English, B/C/S page 45 - that when -- and I can say as we're waiting for that to come up, that when the grave was first exhumed in 1996, 140 bodies were found. And over the next many years, many secondary graves connected to that grave were found. And the total, as we can see from the B/C/S on your side of the page, and this is called Branjevo Pilica, was 1.751. And if -- you may know that Erdemovic also testified that there were approximately 500 Muslim men being kept at the cultural centre in Pilica that were also executed. And we have evidence in this case that they too were buried at the Branjevo farm. So if you add in that estimate -- both those estimates of Erdemovic, 500 at Pilica and 1.000 to 1200 at the farm, you get almost very close to the actual number that some 18 years later after the work started we now have. So if that's correct, you'd have to admit that Erdemovic was very good in his estimates, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell precisely now either about Erdemovic or the other five in Sarajevo who claimed the number was lower. But if these are the statistics and they are correct, I have to agree that this is the number of bodies. Now, whether the six men from the 10th Detachment executed all of them or not, I can't tell, but I can't believe that six men could have executed so many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, did you know that they had help from people, as described by Erdemovic, that were from Bratunac, a unit that came and helped them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the statements of the young men who gave evidence in Sarajevo, I know that some of them were also involved. I also asked in February to May 1996, but they didn't know who these men were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, where exactly are we -- are you referring to the denial of the numbers, et cetera, what are we talking about in terms of the statement of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have the exact reference, but I think he'll agree he said that he didn't think the numbers were very high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did he say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that was in his testimony the previous day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, then I must have missed that. Yes. Then I'll check that, because it's -- because there is -- in itself, there is not much use, someone who has no direct knowledge, to go through the evidence which is before the Chamber and then ask the witness to evaluate more or less what is true or what is not true. That's -- if he has any personal knowledge, that's fine. If he analyses the evidential materials, then he can easily leave it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Could we go to D320 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'm going back briefly, Mr. Pelemis, to the 11 July period, and what you should see is an order. And I think we can see from the -- from this original Serbian, is that your signature or someone else's for you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franc Kos signed for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And is this an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see number 19 on this list, a Zoran Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there was a mistake last week when I mentioned the nickname of the person that slit the Muslim's throat. It was a mistake in the transcripts which was cleared up by Mr. Stojanovic in Erdemovic's testimony at page 13741, when he said: "The incident with the killing of a male that you talked about by a man named Maljic," M-a-l-j-i-c, "had already occurred before General Mladic arrived; is that correct?" And he said: "Yes." So the nickname that we are talking about is for Zoran Obrenovic and it's a well-known nickname for him named Maljic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maljic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's Zoran Obrenovic's nickname?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's the man that slit the throat of the Muslim on your orders in Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the man, because that man was at the command of the division in the Dom and he wasn't present at the centre. And I repeat, I did not order the murder of that civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another subject. I'm sure you'll acknowledge an operation that you and your unit went on in June of 1995 through the tunnel into Srebrenica town. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's go to P1585. And the second page. Go to the next page, please. Page 3 in the B/C/S. And in the English, the centre of the page, if we could blow that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is the UNPROFOR report on your mission. "A group of unknown strength set up firing positions on two locations" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are we reading, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The right in the middle, the big middle paragraph under "Reconstruction of events."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "... (where the launch tubes were found). They fired their projectile simultaneously into Srebrenica. One man was injured when the projectile struck his house. After the attack, personnel of the firing teams retreated to the mine entrance under cover of mortar fire. 19 grenades were fired from the vicinity of the mine entrance. It is not sure whether another mortar from outside the enclave delivered supporting fire. The people fled from their house in Vitlovac near the mine entrance in the direction of Srebrenica. They probably surprised some of the people of the raid group who were waiting near the mine entrance. They were shot with an M," it's unclear, "killing the woman and injuring the man. The raid group probably retreated through the mine." So your entrance into the mine, fired Zoljas into the town, and you killed a woman on your way out.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not go into Srebrenica in order to fire at it. Instead, we targeted the police station, the command of the brigade, and the communications centre; that is to say, the post office. After the completion of the operation, nobody reported to me that they had noticed even one person in the street, and I don't understand how this woman came to be killed. The order was, during our movement, pay special attention not to fire at civilian houses. We targeted insulations of the 28th Division and the military authorities in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, the first -- or, as a matter of fact, the second line of your quote says: "They fired their projectile." May I take it that everyone agrees that it says "projectiles," the S is not very visible, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Mr. President, for catching that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might also add, somewhere you said that people fled. It's "two people fled," this man and that woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 32371.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the purpose of this mission into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose and the objective was -- since the forces of the 28th Division of the Muslim army kept making incursions from the area, killing civilians and people around Srebrenica, the order had come that we have to fire at their command in order to reduce these raids and the killing of civilians in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the handwriting in this document? This came to us from the state court.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is this that you're doing here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about the sabotage operations that we carried out. It says "Franc Kos, leader." The second member is Drazen Erdemovic, Mladen Filipovic, Matija Marinovic, and Aris Leferis. That is the usual composition of the 10th Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we see there is various names, Orkan, and they are dated -- you've written in December 1994. And then there is one that's illegible from 1995, and then there is 20 February 1995. Are these different operations or ... and we can look at the next page as well.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, can we go to the next page. This is not very legible. This is better. Yes, this is a conventional coding of sabotage actions and their participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see the top here, "Regional Water Supply ..."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this document, when did you draft it? When did you draw it up?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime after the war. After the signing of the Dayton Accords. I analysed everything based on the documentation in the archives of the 10th Sabotage Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you get the archives of the 10th Sabotage Unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was taken from me, from my apartment, when the state security services of Serbia searched my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I thought you'd just said you'd drafted this after the war based on the archives of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. My question was: Where did you have access to the archives of the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those documents were in the 10th Sabotage Detachment when I was its commander. And I wrote this during my change-over, when I was removed from my position. But all the archives were in the command of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. What is missing here is financial reports, i.e., how much compensation each of the members received, and the report of the group commander on the success of each of the actions. So that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this water-supply, what city was that water supply for?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the regional water-supply for Tuzla. However, because of the civilians at the reception, it was decided not to blow up the water-supply itself but the bridge leading to the water-supply in order to avoid casualties and substantial damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why would you blow up a water-supply in the first place for a civilian town? And I -- I'm -- of course, there is military in the town as well.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what my superior command in the intelligence administration knew. Can you hear me? I could not discuss what the administration knew and why the regional water-supply was important at all. I also couldn't discuss, nor anybody could, when the television building in Belgrade was bombed in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just seek clarification of the last answer. The bombing of the television building in Belgrade, bombing by -- you mean by NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, why couldn't you discuss that? I mean, you're not asked to discuss it, but what is it that makes you think that you could not discuss that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was in a position of the person who had received the order to bomb the television building. I was in that position. I got an order to blow up the regional water-supply on a condition that civilian casualties were avoided. The action was not carried out after all. I really don't see why this water-supply should appear as a problem. That never materialised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you say you got an order to blow up the regional water-supply, avoiding civilian casualties, and you didn't do it. Is that -- so apparently you were in a discussion -- in a position to form your own opinion on whether this was legal or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Every action, not just that one. If an action targeting military targets put civilians in jeopardy, then such an action would be aborted. It happened on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this seems to be not exactly the same as what you told us before, that you were not in a position to discuss these kind of matters. Do you remember how your superiors reacted when you apparently did not, as you said, follow the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing. There was a little house next to the water-supply, there were civilians there, possibly refugees. That's what we told them. There was no comment. The only reaction we received was: All right, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why then blow up the bridge? I mean, what was the purpose. If you're ordered to blow up a water-supply and then you end up blowing up a bridge, why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because that road was used by military units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had not received an order to destruct the -- that road? To destroy that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but there is always an order which says: If the primary target cannot be destroyed, then there is a secondary target that has to be taken into consideration as a possible target. And again, I'm talking about military facilities, not civilian facilities or civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you specifically were instructed or ordered to blow up the bridge if you couldn't blow up the water-supply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the order was to blow up the water-supply. In case that was not feasible, a minor target was designated in order to inflict some damage on the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that order given in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nothing in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We see in front of us under number 9, the Srebrenica tunnel incursion of June of 1995. And these are your notes still, are they not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we've seen from the UN report that you managed to hit civilian structures when you fired your rockets or your RPGs or your Zoljas, whatever they were. What were they that you fired in -- into the town?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that one house was hit. It was a Zolja, a 64-millimetre Zolja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see here that you went into the town and your action caused panic and disarray among the civilian population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not civilian population but the command of the 28th Division and Brigade, and this was a warning to them not to make anymore incursions and stop killing Serbs around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if you say "and we can see here," I think from what I read nothing says that there was the -- "panic and disarray was among the civilian population." So you should clearly distinguish between what we see, as you put it to the witness, and what may be the position of the Prosecution although which we cannot see on the document. We should, in order to avoid any confusion, be clear on that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you fired your Zoljas into the town, into an inhabited village, striking a house. The purpose of this was to scare the daylights out of the civilians and cause panic and disarray among the civilians, among the military, among everyone, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. 50 people passed through Vidikovac between Muslim houses. It was never our goal, it was never our intention to kill a single civilian. If that had been our intention, we could have killed all the people in the settlement. We entered through a settlement where there were at least 300 or 400 people and we came back the same way. Nobody was harmed. We targeted those facilities which were mapped out for us, we knew what they were. If a single Zolja missed its target at 3.00 in the morning, it's a different story. I don't know who may have fired it and how that happened, but it was not intentionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the Zolja was fired by accident, is that what you're saying, not intentionally?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Zolja was fired with an intention to strike one of the three or four targets that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'd offer this 65 ter 32371 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7272, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's go on to another subject and let's see your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's D978. It should be page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can see here in paragraph 2 that you say: "From 20 May until August 1992, I was in an independent company which held positions towards Kladanj." And then you say: "In August 1992, an assault detachment was formed based in Vlasenica and I was in that detachment until March 1993," and it goes on. Where were you located in this independent company say that you were in from 20 May until August?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Independent Company Pelemisi had 90 men, and it was deployed on the front line in the direction of Kladanj. Our defence line was 4 or 5 kilometres long. We were the only village in Kladanj municipality which remained standing where civilians had not been killed and where the houses had not be torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to be clear, what village was that that you were talking about defending?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village was Pelemisi, 1 kilometre away from the Tuzla-Kladanj road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so when you described your independent company, it was the Independent Company Pelemisi which had 90 men?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It belonged to the 1st Birac Brigade Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the company or the Birac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Pelemisi Unit.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 24th of May until sometime around the 20th of August - i.e., for two months - I was its commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And during that time-period who was the commander of the Birac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was Svetozar Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go to a map, 65 ter 32342. And so can you describe this -- the village of Pelemisi? First of all, was it your family village in some way?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The village had some 30 houses and it was on the front line; i.e., the front line past through the first couple of houses. My whole family lived there. My mother herself lived on the front line, a couple hundred metres from the trench. We were attacked some five or six times, and before the 1st August we'd had several dozens of killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I just want to orient us a bit with this. This is a map, it's from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could blow up the Serbian map just a little bit. And unfortunately, we didn't get the English title of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you read the title of the map, the Cyrillic? Or what it says?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is there in the English version, although the English version does not -- I don't get it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you read that Cyrillic title on the map?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Deployment of troops on both sides, as at 1st November, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is the bigger map, and I want to go to another 65 ter that will give us a bit of a blow up which is 32343. And if we could just use the Serbian map for the full screen and blow that up if we can. A little bit more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You'll agree with me that in the centre of this map with a red flag, it says the -- it's the Birac Infantry Brigade Sekovici?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is it possible to blow it up a bit more. One more, please. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you see Pelemisi in there? It should be -- it's right between the blue and the red lines. The --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you circle that for us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be provided with a pen so as to circle it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And a bit to the right of this, beyond the red lines, we see Trnovo. Is Pelemisi considered in the general Trnovo area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Before the war, Trnovo belonged to Sekovici and Pelemisi belonged to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to offer this map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7273, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And while you were in command of this 90-person unit, did you hold Muslim prisoners at Pelemisi? In the Pelemisi village or the immediate vicinity of Pelemisi?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in June, the chief of the police station in Kladanj, Stanimir Pelemis, and some of my relatives, since four police officers were taken prisoner in Kladanj on the 23rd of May, before the conflict ended, on the 24th and the 25th, when the Muslims occupied all the Serb villages and all the Serbs fled, we did not have any place to accommodate people and we sent them to Sekovici. Stanimir Pelemis and the relatives of those who went missing from Kladanj, some 28 of them all together, addressed the police station in Vlasenica and brought some six or seven women and four or five men for exchange. I could not turn them down and I gave them a possibility to carry out the exchange. I know that on two occasions they sent Muslim women to Kladanj to talk about the exchange, but it all fell through. And then I told Radenko Zoranovic, since his brother and two relatives were among them, and I told him if the exchange failed to return all the Muslim people where they had come from. I know that the Muslim women were returned to Vlasenica and the men stayed in Trnovo and joined the battalion. On the 20th August, I left the area. And after that, I did not have any authority nor did I know what was going on. I just need to say something else. In the month of July, from the direction of Vlasenica, sometime during the night two buses arrived and brought Muslims, and those people from Trnovo and Pelemis escorted those 120 people who went in the direction of Kladanj. After that, I called the commander, Commander Andric, and I told him to warn those people from Vlasenica to stop bringing people across the line, across my line, because there was also a highway leading from Vlasenica to Kladanj. This is all I know about the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So your commander, Andric, was also aware that there were women at Pelemisi at this point?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he did. I believe that all that was organised along the police line, that the Sekovici police station was involved. Those were all policemen. Since I was never in Kladanj, I did not know what it was all about. And they were arrested one day before the operation started, and then they tried to exchange them. That never materialised. And in 1997, we found them in the village of Bretelovici [phoen] near Kladanj. They had all been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I just ask a clarification, what does that mean "to bring someone for exchange"? Is that you offer your own people for exchange or is it that you bring persons from the opposite side and suggest that they should be exchanged for your own people? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The policemen who left Kladanj and found themselves in Vlasenica offered Muslims to be exchanged for the Serbs who had remained in Kladanj. That's how I understood the whole thing. Your Honour, we did not have any conditions. We did not have even a single cellar, let alone a prison. They lived normally in a place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, you just can release them, isn't it? I mean, to bring civilians for exchange means that you offered them whereas they may have wished otherwise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm only saying that they brought people who said that they wanted the civilians to cross over to the territory of the BiH Army. They wanted to benefit from that, to exchange the Serb civilians who had remained in Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, "exchange" means you want something in return from those who you are offering. If people want to move out, why is there any need for exchange? Just release civilians. Because you shouldn't detain them or put them in a position where they were dependent on whether or not there would be any exchange.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had been asked, I would not have brought them over. I would not have done that. But those were relatives and friends of those who had stayed behind. This is what they tried. And I told them that if they couldn't do it, if they could not speed things along, that they should be returned to Vlasenica because they were a burden for a village on the front line. I did not have food for my own people, let alone others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was -- your own people, did they deserve food and others not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I'm saying is that even my people did not have enough. At the same time, whatever my people had, they had as well. At that time, we did not have any logistics support. Sekovici is a very poor municipality. Whatever stock we had was used very quickly. The point that I'm making is that my own people did not have enough to eat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as you added to that, therefore the others were a burden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even a single mouth on top of all of us was a burden. I made numerous attempts to move out my own people from Pelemisi, especially the old and infirm. Everybody relied on me for sustenance, and I did not have enough. Sekovici was a poor municipality. I begged around to see if somebody could give me flour, salt, and other staples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey. Or if I say so, then I haven't looked at the clock. We'll take a break first. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom. Perhaps I use the time for D920, which was marked for identification on the 2nd of March pending a translation. On the 10th of March, the Defence e-mailed the Chamber and the Prosecution and advised that a translation had been uploaded into e-court, and the Chamber would like to hear from the Prosecution whether it has any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would not be surprised if it received that information after the next break. Meanwhile, Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Pelemis, on page 18 of the temporary transcript, I asked: "And while you were in command of the 90-person unit, did you hold Muslim prisoners in Pelemisi? Or in the Pelemisi village or the immediate vicinity of Pelemisi?" And you went on a bit and then said: "... some 28 of them all together, addressed the police station in Vlasenica and brought some six or seven women and four or five men for exchange. I could not turn them down and I gave them a possibility to carry out the exchange." And how long did those six or seven women and four or five men stay in Pelemisi?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the women stayed for two months and the men stayed longer. They didn't want to go back to Vlasenica. They stayed at Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said about the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You need to repeat what you said about the battalion, if anything. The interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later when the situation calmed down, the company became part of the Trnovo Battalion. I believe that's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Tell me the name of one or more of the women or girls.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any names. Believe me, I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't even know a first name of any of them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, really, I don't remember. Look, I wasn't dealing with it. All I wanted was to make sure that they were safe while there, that they have enough food and medicine. I had other problems because to the right of me, in a 4-kilometre line it was all empty, they were attacking, 50 men per shift, up to 200 men in total. I had to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So as commander it was your duty to protect these females?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the age range of these females?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, there were two or three elderly women, there were three or four young ones. The age range was 20-something to 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about 16 years old? Was there a 16-year-old?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was only one child, 2 or 3 years old, that stayed behind. The mother didn't want to come back for the child.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were some of these women, when they were in Pelemisi, raped repeatedly by you and your troops?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Except one man came from another unit and we turned him over to a different unit, I believe Pekic's company, while we were away on a field mission, and we found out about what he did only when we came back. And all we could do was turn him over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So while you were away on a field mission someone came in and raped some of these women?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: One, I believe. The one that we knew about complained, then we found him and arrested him and turned him over to Trnovo. He was not from our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what was the name of the woman that reported she'd been raped while in your protection?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't remember. Stanimir Pelemis was in charge. He was the chief of the police station in Kladanj, and he was in charge of them, he took care of them and was preparing the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he rape her repeatedly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I believe it was only once. I know that my men gave him a good beating, and that's why I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which one of your men was guarding the place where the woman, the victim, was, inhabited?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe these were not young men. His name was Momir, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was -- Momir was one of your men?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was in the Pelemis Company, Momir Pelemis, and he reported it together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which one of your men was responsible for securing the residence where the victim stayed while you were away?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe no one, because they were all away in the field holding the line near the motorway for two ways. We were making ambushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you had six or seven women that you were responsible -- held in a residence surrounded by soldiers and you had no one protecting them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not responsible directly for them. But I let the police station chief to bring them to the exchange. They were in a facility not together with army troops but among other civilians. It was a regular house owned by a man who was a tradesman, and that's where they slept, in the middle of the settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I won't dwell on this but who was the man who owned the house? And we understand it's your namesake village, it's a tiny village, so tell us who -- who owned the house at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it be Radan? Not a young man. And it's been 25 years, I can't remember. Radan, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The house is still there in Pelemisi, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was razed to the ground back in 1993. Like all the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Muslim troops overran the village and -- and then?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took it five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's Radan's full name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pelemis, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 11377. This is part of a Security Council report. It's an annex referred to as the "Annex to the Final Report of the United Nations Commission of Experts, established pursuant to the Security Council Resolution 780 of 1992." I'd like to go to page 2 in both languages. And we see that this is an annex of rape and sexual assault by Cherif Bassiouni. It's dated 27 May 1994. And if we could go to page 34 in the English, page 77 in the B/C/S. And if we could blow up paragraph 139, entitled "Kladanj."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there is a brief description in the beginning of it, describing where it is and the prewar population of 16.028. According to the 1991 census, Muslims were the majority with 77.3 per cent of the population. Serbs comprised 23.9 per cent. And then I'll read out: "According to one woman from Vlasenica, she and 42 other men, women, and children were taken from Susica camp in Vlasenica on 10 August 1992. They were told they were to be exchanged in Tuzla. However, the women and children were put into a room in a house in Pelemis, Kladanj. There were about 15 women and 10 men in the basement of the house. There, seven girls, ages 14 to 16, were raped two or three times a week, sometimes during the day. No other women were mistreated." Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the number you cited really has nothing to do with what happened while I was there. I said that there were seven to eight women and there was one three-year-old child. I know about one rape and I told you what I did about it and how I dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 32355.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could I just ask for a clarification before we go on. Sir, you said this 3-year-old child's mother didn't want to come back for her. What became of the 3-year-old child finally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The child was later returned. We took her back one and a half years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the place near Tuzla where the exchange took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To whom did you hand the child?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On our side, a family was keeping her. And then after a year, when an exchange took place near Tuzla, the child was probably taken back to the mother. I know that the child is with her mother now and everything ended well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question is to whom was the child handed when he or she was returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the mother, personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what's the name of the family that looked after the child for the year and a half?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vucinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what was the mother's name to whom the child was handed? You should know that one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do you then know that the child was handed to the mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was told by Jerko Vucinovic, who was captured in 1995, and then the mother and child came to visit him in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have no personal knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what do you want to do with the expert report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I'll -- I don't need to enter it into evidence, Your Honour, at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that numbers are referred to which are not part of what is uploaded into e-court. I see number 278 at the end of this Kladanj paragraph, whereas the title is 277. Is that the statement of the person or what does it refer to? You see, it looks as if these are footnotes but I don't find them in the document as uploaded. And this, by the way, appears to be an annex to the report of experts. Or an annex to something else. But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I'd stated it was an annex, in my question, of the expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course. This is very much of a summary, and if there is any way you could get hold of what is apparently here 278, then perhaps we might have a look at it or it depends on what it tells us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll look a bit further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially because, of course, this report, and I take it that you to some extent rely on it to the extent that you have read parts of it, it's not in evidence, but, of course, it may make a difference on who took a statement, if there is a statement, whether that statement supports what is summarised here rather than to just take for granted what is summarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're getting to some more information, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then if you come to that, then we'll wait for that. I'm always a bit impatient perhaps now and then. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No problem. Could we go to 65 ter 32355.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report of an organisation called ICMP, the International Commission for Missing Persons. It's a "Summary Excavation Report" is what it says in English, and it says: "Excavations at Pelemisi, Sekovici, BiH, from 16 to 23 August 2004." And I'm not going to go through all of that, but I do want to show you another -- a brief map and ask you a couple of questions based on some of the information that is in this report. It's 65 ter 32345. And as we're waiting for this map to come up, I can tell you that this report is the report of the exhumation of two mass graves. And this map is a 1:25.000 scale, so as we can see at the bottom each square is 1 kilometre. We can see Pelemisi there. Does that look like the -- your Pelemisi?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I can tell you that in the green -- the little green dot at the map co-ordinates 34TCQ227, et cetera, which is within about a kilometre of the village of Pelemisi, there was a exhumation where 49 people were recovered there, with six women, the youngest being 16 years old. The other exhumation for the northern co-ordinate had at least nine people in it, men. These were Muslim women and a girl. Are these the six females you spoke about, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the mass graves, I made some inquiries with my men who had been on the line as to what had happened. Sometime near September or October, they noticed buses coming in the night. They reported it to the superior command, requesting the command to prevent those paramilitaries from Vlasenica arriving. I really don't know who was buried in the mass graves. Before the 22 August, when I was the Pelemisi Company commander, nobody was killed because I would not allow something like that to happen. But I am fully prepared to co-operate with the prosecutor's office of the BiH court in their investigation as to who did that and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you were the commander of the Pelemisi Detachment in October of 1992, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 32372. And for the purposes of these questions, Your Honours, I don't believe it's necessary to offer any of this material into evidence. I think it's clear what it is and what I'm asking about, unless the Court would like it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the map in itself, we don't need that. I don't know yet what all this material is, so I have difficulties in -- it's up to you finally, Mr. McCloskey, to tender it or not to tender it. If you tender it, we include it with all its details in the evaluation of the evidence. If you don't do it, then everything we know is what you read from it. And we take it that if something is read, Mr. Lukic, that if there is no objection, that it reflects what the document tells us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, on second thought, I -- at the end I will reconsider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'm almost to the end, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you've acknowledged, the Muslims overran your positions, and we believe this is a recovered document. Though -- you can see that this is a document from the Pelemisi Detachment, your name typed into it, and a signature. That's your signature, isn't it? We can blow it up a bit if you want to see it more.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not my signature. However, I did issue such certificates. I can give you an explanation. On the 1st of September, I was appointed the commander of the assault detachment. I was in Vlasenica. These are certificates for my men. They wanted to resort to my influence when they addressed the authorities in Vlasenica and elsewhere for the allocation of apartments, because their houses had been destroyed in bombing. On the 23rd of October, Pelemisi Detachment was a company, not a detachment, and I was the commander of the assault detachment. And here I am saying that I put my signature on the certificates because my name would be their ticket to obtaining places to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this is your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This is not my signature. I am saying that this particular signature is not mine, but I did sign certificates of this nature for my family and others. I am not denying that I issued certificates of this kind because I tried to help everybody who needed accommodation, but this is not the way I sign my name. Maybe somebody tried to falsify my signature if they needed a house. But I'm not denying that I signed such documents for my father, my uncle, and others from the village because they had lost everything in the village and they needed accommodation somewhere in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're pretending you're the detachment commander in having this kind of document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was the commander of the assault detachment. Maybe it's not clear from this particular document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But, sir, what's very clear --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but from the 1st of September --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's very clear from this document is that this is from the Pelemisi Detachment, we see that right at the top, and right at the bottom it says "Detachment Commander, Milorad Pelemis." So are you saying, this document, you're pretending to be the Pelemisi Detachment? We've heard of the assault position.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't pretend. Everybody knew that I was the commander of the assault detachment in Vlasenica. I handed over my duties on the 20th of August. This is not my signature. Somebody misused my signature. But I did issue certificates of this kind when people needed accommodation. This is not my signature. If I had been offered this document to sign, I would have signed it to help those people who did not have a roof over their head. My mother, for example, lived 100 metres away from the front lines. She had spent six months living in a cellar. Why would not -- why wouldn't I have signed a document for my mother? I don't mind if somebody would have signed -- forged my signature on my mother's document. What should I have done, leave my mother in the cellar to starve or to be raped by Muslims when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tell me, if you were going to help your mother or other Serbs, why wouldn't you write such a certificate with your actual position, which I take was a promotion from this position? Why would you have to fake it to your own people?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that this is not my signature. It's a fake signature. When I sign such a document, I signed it as the commander of the assault detachment, and I stand by every such document. And this was signed by somebody else because Boro Milosevic needed a house. If I had been given this document to sign, I would have signed it. I repeat: I would have because I wanted people to be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could I ask you a few questions about when we started this whole exercise about who was in what position in October. Witness, you said you made some inquiries with the men who had been on the line as to what happened to those which were found in the mass graves. You said: "... they noticed buses coming in the night. They reported it to the superior command ..." Which superior command they reported the arrival of buses coming in the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that I had said that. When the mass graves were opened in 2004, I spoke to the commanders of the platoons and detachments, those who were on the line at that time, and they told me that at that time vehicles would arrive from Vlasenica during the night. There were police officers on those buses, and they executed people from Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They asked for help --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down and continue. So: "... and they executed people from Vlasenica," and could you please resume from there? Who asked for help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our commanders and those people who were on the line asked the superior command for help. They wanted them to prevent the Vlasenica police from doing such things behind our line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was: Which was the superior command they, as you said, reported -- they reported to? Which was that superior command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police station in Sekovici and the command of the 1st Birac Brigade in Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said you made some inquiries with your men who had been on the line. So as a matter of fact, you were the superior command at that moment, not the police, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, why do you then say "my men" if they were not your men, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were people who had --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness should slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. The interpreters are unable to follow you. So "those were people who had," and could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who had been in the war with me from day one. They started by defending our village from the enemy. They will always be my brothers, they will always be my men. These are primarily my relatives from the village. I consider them my brethren, I consider them my men. They were the first line up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who was their superior command, if it weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The battalion in Trnovo and the command in Sekovici. That was the line, the Pelemisi Detachment reports to the Trnovo Battalion, and the Trnovo Battalion reports to the Sekovici command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did they report in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. It was the battalion command that drafted its reports in writing. I am not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if you don't know, that's good enough. What did you do with that information once you had received that after the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the exhumation, I spoke to the investigators who were involved with the case. I told them that I was willing to share with them all I knew and I had learned from the people who were there and perhaps could offer some information about the mass graves that had been discovered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Investigators from what authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And was any statement taken from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They said that they would send me an official invitation to come to Belgrade for an interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Bosnia and Herzegovina investigators inviting you to come to Belgrade. Were you living in Serbia at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did not understand me. I've lived in Serbia since 1982, but I told the investigators in Bosnia that I was willing to help them shed light on those crimes and to tell them what I learned from my men who were on the line at the time, which was in autumn 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you then invited and did you speak with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was told that I would be informed about everything and that they would talk to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it never happened. Is that what I have to understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We spoke some two years ago, and then they said that they would come to Belgrade ex officio and that they would talk to me. I'm still at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two years ago. I missed perhaps the information. Do the parties have any information about when the exhumation took place? It's my recollection that a date far back was used. Do you -- perhaps the witness. Do you remember when that exhumation took place which caused you to make further inquiries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was shown a document just a while ago, and I could see that the year was 2004. That's when the exhumation took place. There was a document on the screen just a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's also your recollection, that it happened in 2004?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If I had not seen the year on the document, I would have completely forgotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said you'd talked to them two years ago, that is, in 2013. What did you -- when did you offer your assistance to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, two years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you knew about it since most likely 2004, because you said when the exhumation had taken place, you further inquired into the matter and you heard all kind of things from what you called your men. When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was immediately after the exhumation. I wanted to know whether any of them had participated in that. They categorically denied. And they said that the people involved were from Vlasenica, from the police and some paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question now is: Approximately some nine or ten years elapsed since you inquired and since, as you said, you had spoken to these investigators. My earlier question was: What did you do with that information, and you said you talked to investigators. But do I now understand that you talked after nine or ten years to investigators rather than immediately after you found out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not immediately after that. There was no need because I heard from my people that had not participated in that. I was not in a position to conduct an investigation in Bosnia from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You heard meanwhile that the police in Vlasenica was responsible for those killings. That's what you told us. Didn't you consider that relevant to bring to the attention of the investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not been in Bosnia for over ten years. I don't know how I could help the investigators from Belgrade. I spoke to them indirectly through my lawyers. I offered them my services with regard to those two graves. The most important thing for me, Your Honour, was that nobody from the Pelemis Company who was on the line didn't participate in that crime. Your Honour, I'm unemployed, I don't have any means to participate in any investigation, let alone an investigation taking place in Bosnia and Herzegovina given that I am in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you can take the phone, call to whomever, and say, "I have additional information. I learned that the Vlasenica police committed those killings for which in 2004 human remains were exhumed." Is that -- you don't need that much money for that, one phone call, and apparently you had all the means to inquire with your men.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know is where the company members were at the time. I don't know who exactly from Vlasenica did it. I don't know their names. They only told me that they were the police and paramilitaries. I don't know what else I could say about the perpetrators of the crime. I can only tell the investigators who was on the line, who has some information, who may have been eye-witnesses of whatever. That's the extent of my assistance to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what then triggered after nine or ten years to speak with these investigators where for nine or ten years you considered it totally useless to do that? Why then two years ago you ... what happened that you got in touch with them, what happened that you started offering your assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing. I spoke to a lawyer from Republika Srpska and he told me that if I wished to do so, I could convey what I know about that crime. He gave me a number that I could call. I did call it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What triggered you to be in touch with a lawyer from Republika Srpska? What happened that triggered that advice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if somebody says that there was a grave in Pelemisi, it wasn't. It was between the villages of Trnovo and Pelemisi in the mountains there. Well, just so that nobody could say this was done in Pelemisi by the Pelemisi men. That was what prompted me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you knew that for nine or ten years already. What then triggered you to go and see a lawyer in Republika Srpska after having had this knowledge for nine or ten years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not go to Republika Srpska. The lawyer was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You talked about a lawyer from Republika Srpska. Even if you didn't see him in Republika Srpska, that's deviating from what's the core of my question. What triggered you to consult a lawyer from Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lawyer was there on official business. We talked. I asked him whether I would be able to shed some light on that crime because the mass graves had been found there. He gave me a number and told me to call them because they would probably want to interview me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, you just happened to see a Republika Srpska lawyer in Belgrade, which you happened to have a conversation with, and then you told him something which you knew already for nine or ten years, and then he advised you that they would probably want to interview you. Has it got anything to do with your name being mentioned in proceedings in Republika Srpska which would have triggered that you felt that you might have been targeted by the investigators yourself and that for that reason you consulted a lawyer? Is that what may have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not exactly. I know that some other people from Vlasenica tried to blame me to no avail, and that's the part that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that triggered you to have a conversation with that lawyer. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, more or less so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why didn't you give this answer two pages earlier? Why didn't you immediately tell, "I consulted that lawyer because others had mentioned my name in this context and that caused me to see this lawyer," instead of saying, "I just happened to meet a lawyer and we had a conversation," where apparently, if I understand you well, you sought to consult that lawyer because - and there is nothing wrong with that - your name had been mentioned by others who blamed you for all kind of things? Why didn't you give that answer immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not seek lawyers. I just happened to talk to a lawyer who was in Belgrade. I talked to him and he gave me advice as to what I could do in legal terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you learn that you were blamed for anything? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some lads from Vlasenica who were interrogated. The investigators put questions about me as to where I was at the time, which unit I commanded, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When were they interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some two, three, or four years ago. I can't remember. Within the last three years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So shortly before you had this conversation with a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you pay the lawyer for his services, advising you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You got it for free?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the name of that lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Golic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you happen to know why he was in Belgrade then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was involved in a civil case. He represented a company in Republika Srpska or something of that kind. I did not ask too many questions. And he is from Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you contact him or did he contact you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He contacted me through friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for what reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He suggested that we just meet up since he was coming to Belgrade, and we went to a cafe and sat together. But we know each other from back during the war. We knew each other only superficially, though, not very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are we close to break time? I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are close to break time, and I do acknowledge that when you said that you were close to the time you would finish that I took -- that I postponed that moment by my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nope, I -- if I could just offer that document into evidence. It is 65 ter 32372.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7274, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I have another document or two and a very short video-clip, and so I think I should be done in ten minutes if ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we could continue for another ten minutes which would give you an opportunity to know all of the cross-examination before you start the re-examination, but I'm quite willing to take the break now immediately and perhaps you want to consult with Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know how my colleague would like to proceed. It's his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's one. And second, Mr. McCloskey --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't mind to continue [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes of Mr. McCloskey is not necessarily always ten minutes. Mr. McCloskey, shall we continue -- shouldn't we continue after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That way I'll try to un-McCloskey-ise my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was nevertheless happy with the ten minutes announced and I would encourage you to make it really ten minutes. We take a break and we will resume at quarter past midday, after the witness has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was a matter to be raised by the parties but not immediately, if I understand well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. I understand the Defence also had something to raise. Mr. Registrar suggested that we both wait until after the witness concluded his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there was one outstanding -- I think it was about the D920, whether there were any objections to the new translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was one of the issues. Since the Court raised it now, I can tell you that we have no objection to the translation itself. However, we, despite our efforts, have been unable to find the point during his testimony when the witness discussed the actual document and would therefore ask the Defence for the page reference with respect to that particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you'll provide that, Mr. Lukic, to the Prosecution. Meanwhile, Mr. McCloskey, your ten minutes have started, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you'd just said back, I believe page 40 to 41: "Some other people from Vlasenica tried to blame me." Blame you for what?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to those graves that were found in Kladanj, behind Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Give me the names of the people that you believe have blamed you for the crimes associated with the graves.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to give the names. I'll tell the investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, would you please answer the question that was put to you by Mr. McCloskey. If there is any specific reasons why you don't want to give those names in a public session, you can ask for private session, but you are -- you have to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not 100 per cent certain about all of them. When I get some certainty, I will provide their names. I'm not sure at this moment that some of those people tried to shift the buck onto me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we are not going to wait until you have your certainty as you wish to seek it. The names you are aware of, even though you are not certain yet, we'd like to hear them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I have only one name, a man called Kraljevic from Vlasenica, whom I know only slightly. I heard that he had given a statement and that he wants to shift responsibility to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say: "When I get some certainty I'll provide their names," so apparently you have more names on your mind. Could you give us the other names, even though not being certain, but what you are aware of at this moment as the names of persons that may have blamed you for something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell you now. I remember now only the name of this Kraljevic who tried to shift some responsibility onto me. But when I go back home, I'll try to get all the names. Because I really don't know people from Vlasenica. We don't have good contacts at all. For instance, from 1993 to this day, my mother got housing only three months ago. Until now, she lived in community housing. And she got an apartment now only because she had suffered a stroke. If I had any contacts there, I would have secured an apartment at least ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- however important it may be, it's not directly related to my questions. I offered to you that you could give the names in private session or at least that we would consider that if you would have asked for it. You preferred not to do that.
