I repeat that if any of the other names, and you told us about names, in the plural, that if you would like to move into private session to give the other names, that we would consider that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need. For now I know only the name of Mico Kraljevic. I cannot allow myself to make a mistake. There was a lot of talk. But about this one name, I heard about him from many different people. I tried even to discuss it with him, but he avoids seeing me. I am sure that he tried to shift some blame onto me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I read part of one of your previous answers. You said: "I'm not a hundred per cent certain about all of them. When I get some certainty, I will provide their names," in the plural. Your most recent answer that you don't remember the other names at least requires some explanation in view of your previous answer. If you want to give that, you can do it now. Otherwise, I'll invite Mr. McCloskey to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honestly, Judge, I'm sure about this man. As for the rest, you know, it's he says, she says. I would like to run my own checks. I don't want to blame falsely other people. I'm certain about this one and I invited him to come and talk to me. As for others, I don't know. For now I have only one name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "I don't want to blame falsely other people." If you have no names, you couldn't even do that. I asked you for an explanation. The explanation you've given is on the record. Mr. McCloskey may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you refusing to give us names of such people, particularly Muslim names, so that you are free to intimidate them or greater in case a case against you comes to trial?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What Muslims? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're not aware that any Muslims have made any allegations against you regarding the killings and rapings in Pelemisi?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I really have no contact with them, and I don't know anyone who would know me from Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So all these years, from 1992, with all the statements and all the reports, you're not aware of any Muslims that have said anything against you regarding the crimes in the summer and fall of 1992 in Pelemisi?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to offer into evidence, given this involved testimony of the excavation, the short summary excavation report, which is 65 ter 32355.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we will get a B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You read the mind, at least, of the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P7275, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would also like to enter into evidence 65 ter 32345, and that would be the map that identifies the co-ordinates of the mass grave within -- one of them within the kilometre of Pelemisi. That's the co-ordinates provided in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7276, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is the map. Is that the one marked -- no, that's not the one marked by the witness. No. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The one marked is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is already in evidence. With his markings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's only the one with the markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, Exhibit P7276 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And lastly as a document into evidence, the brief segment of the annex of the Bassiouni report, 65 ter 11377, and we will continue to look if -- see if there is more information on that particular incident that's within the main body of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the brief segment has been uploaded as such? Because it's a lengthy document, the whole of the annex, and we only need ... then we'll reserve a number for the page -- or Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would object, Your Honour, to admission of part of this report since there is no way for us at this moment to check anything on that. There is no names, there is nothing. So if there is some follow-up documentation, we can consider it. But right now to have just this paragraph into evidence, what can we do with that? There is somebody taking some statements from somebody. And allegedly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- condensed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I was only at the point that I said we have dealt with only one page. So the first question I put was whether the single page had been uploaded, and then of course we would consider whether it's ready for admission, yes or no. And you may have noticed that the Chamber, by asking for an explanation of what looks as footnotes, had thoughts which go in the same direction as you have. What we could do is to reserve a number and then leave it to the parties later to exchange views on admission. And perhaps that is better done once you have clarified the footnote issue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's a good idea. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the Defence would know what material underlying the report exists and on what the report relies. I think there were two footnotes in the relevant paragraph. And we'd just reserve a number for the time being and then further hear the parties on admissibility of that portion and possibly any underlying documents. Mr. Registrar, the number reserved for an extract still to be made from this annex of the UN report of experts would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7277, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is reserved for this purpose. Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pelemis, do you recall attending a one-year anniversary of the 10th Sabotage Detachment in Vlasenica? General Krstic attended, Vujadin Popovic attended, and others.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This will be the last exhibit. It's 65 ter 26123C. Janet can play that for us. And there should be subtitles, so we should only play it once. I may ask it be stopped a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, subtitles are in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do they -- is it comment or is it the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be dialogue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be a dialogue. And then of course whether the subtitles accurately interpret what is said has not been verified then yet. Therefore, since there are subtitles and therefore there is a kind of an interpretation, Mr. Lukic, I would like you to carefully look at whether you have any concerns about the accuracy of the English text below, and then at this moment we'll just rely on what is written there up till the moment that we hear from you. And then if it's -- if it will be admitted, it's part of the evidence. Do you have a transcription of the footage if you would tender this later?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And the booths have it. And I know Mr. Lukic can contact Mr. Stojanovic. This has been -- this transcript and this footage has been around for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's look at it and see whether we can do with one round of playing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who are these fellas?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We stopped at 13.7 seconds. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you identify the -- we're at 26.1 now. Can you identify the individuals in this frame? If you could begin with the person first in the frame with the moustache.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember his name was Savo, and he was doing bureaucratic work in the unit. On the left of him is General Krstic, and after Krstic myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We stopped at 26.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We -- you may be able to hear, we can see from the English subtitles that this is a promotion to the rank of reserve infantry sergeant to Drazen Erdemovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the B/C/S has not gotten to that point yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we continue to play it from 47.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Stopping at 1:00.8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was that correct? Was the announcement of a promotion for Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell who that is at 1:08.6?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second-Lieutenant Franc Kos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we're at 02:28.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we've just heard General Krstic pass on the acclaim for you from the commander, and that would have been General Ratko Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Krstic was representing the commander at that time, because everybody was engaged in Western Krajina, so Krstic came on behalf of the command to participate in our celebration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in October of 1995, when Krstic passes on these words from General Mladic, all the Muslims had been dead and buried at the Branjevo farm for many months; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, three or four months, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this would have been something that General Mladic would have been fully aware of in October 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what General Mladic was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President. And I would like this segment in. We can -- it's a bit longer than it is here, but this -- I think this will do it and we'll get that set up so we have a good number for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud, Mr. Mladic. Apparently Mr. Mladic wants to consult with counsel, which he can do at inaudible volume. And we'll wait to start with the re-examination until the consultation has been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bear with me, Your Honours, for half a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is number 26123C. If we could get a number for that, I think we'd be in good shape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm always a bit concerned in portions were not played in court and are nevertheless in evidence. Could you tell us what is left out, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There is only 45 seconds left. If that comes within my ten minutes, we can play it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid that verifying it another way would take far more time. So let's have a look at the last 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Starting on the far left of the frame, that's Svetozar Kosoric, chief of intel for the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Kosoric was in the radio intelligence section of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I thought that when we would look at the last 45 seconds that there would be no further questions about it. But if you want to identify persons, leave it to that. That's okay, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Certain people I can't resist, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us the next one that's in this photograph, the second person from the left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean the person in the second row?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He looks like he's standing behind the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Popovic, the security man from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we had stopped at 02:44.7. And we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, let me see whether a number was already -- no, no number was yet assigned. Mr. Registrar, 26123C would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7278, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pelemis, good day.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have D320 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor asked you today about this document. You said it was signed Franc Kos. This is an order to march. How many groups do you see on that list and who are the leaders of the groups?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see three groups. Group one, that's first squad, Second-Lieutenant Franc Kos. It has seven men. The second group, Drazen Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second group, Drazen Erdemovic. It has ten men. And the third combat group, a squad, Luka Jokic, sergeant, about ten men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you remove Drazen Erdemovic's rank?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never gave it to him, so it was not up to me to remove it. It was the personnel administration of the Main Staff that did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of July, 1995, when the relevant events took place, was Drazen Erdemovic a sergeant as it says in the document or not, as he claims?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He signed a contract with the Ministry of Defence, i.e., the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and that's where he was given his rank. This was one rank, and then he was promoted as we could see in the video-clip and he became a staff sergeant. But if you are asking me specifically about the 10th of June, he was sergeant by rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you say "June" or "July"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: July. I'm looking at the document. It was issued on the 10th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'd like to call up P1585.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to jog your memory about something. This is a report by DutchBat staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are interested in page 2. I apologise. It should be page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Look at the title, "Reconstruction of Events." As you heard, a woman was killed and a man was wounded. I would also like to show you another document about that, P1588. We can see that this was sent by the intelligence administration of the sector for intelligence and security of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska on 21 June 1995. This is an order for the engagement of the 10th Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S, we are on a good page. And in English, we need to go to the next page. We're interested in bullet point 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says, under 6: "In carrying out the task, strictly adhere to the following:" The first entry: "There should be no danger to UNPROFOR members;" The second entry: "Avoid causing casualties among women and children;" And this relates to what operation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The passage through Sase mine and fire opened on the targets of the 28th Division on the 23rd of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were men kept abreast of those items in the order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before they entered the mine in Sase, I read them to my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under 3, I can see in the case of wounding or death of any detachment member, their bodies have to be salvaged at all costs. No member of ours should fall into the enemy hands.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a rule for every unit. Even if five died, we had to salvage their bodies, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were shown the maps of Pelemisi and the area around it. I believe that something was not recorded precisely on page 16, line 25, where you mentioned the number of dead in defence. When you were in charge of the defence of Pelemisi village, how many people got killed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: 49 or 50, between the 24th of May and the 20th of August. And that concerns all the fighters in my units and those who arrived to help us. All in all, about 50 got killed during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On transcript page 20, line 12, you started saying something about the people who were accommodated in the village who had been brought there to be exchanged. You said that you did not have any conditions in place. You didn't even have -- and the rest of your answer was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any logistics support. This is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have cells where people could be kept in that village?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we just had simple houses and they were all inhabited by the local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, those people who had been brought there, were they accommodated in empty houses or were -- did they join the Serbs living in them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that guy lived there and then he moved in with his brother, so those people were accommodated in his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how long did the people stay there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 15 or 20 days while I was there. Or perhaps up to a month. And then after all the exchange attempts failed, they were taken back to Vlasenica. At that time in Kladanj, we had 220 Serbs in various camps, and we didn't know what was happening to them. And that attempt to exchange those people and save them, that was what the former police station in Kladanj was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And those people who were accommodated in that house, who provided food for them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one day it was one house and the other it was another. As they got friendlier with the people, they would provide for them, and the military did the same at the time. Everybody made do as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I'm going to have another intervention on the transcript. It doesn't mean anything to you when I say page 23, line 23. You said 50 men in a shift. A total of -- how many men did you have in total?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, if I say that we had 90 people in the list, 45 would be in positions and 45 would be resting either for two hours or seven hours, which means that the line was 5 kilometres long and it was manned by 45 men at the time, and that means that defence opportunities were slim. That's why I was on the line 24/7, to keep vigil, to keep my men awake, and to make sure that we were not surprised by the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I would like to return to the previous subject which you have apparently concluded. You answered questions about a number, if I understand it well, a considerable number of persons who would be -- who were to be exchanged, and then you were asked where they were accommodated, whether it was in empty houses, and whether they did join the Serbs living in those houses. And then your answer was: "I believed that that guy lived there and then he moved in with his brother, so those people were accommodated in his house." Do I understand that that guy who lived there, was that a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the person who moved in, therefore, being his brother, was a Serb as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I understood that the people we were talking about were Muslims to be exchanged, so I'm a bit surprised by those answers, first of all, because you're referring only to one person where we are talking about many more; and second, that I do not understand if asked about accommodation of those persons who were there to be exchanged, how that would be Serbs. Do you have an answer to the two questions; first of all, that you were talking only about the accommodation of one person, and second, how a Serb could be among those to be exchanged? Perhaps you start with the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me clarify. When the six or seven women were brought to Pelemisi to be exchanged, a man, who was a Serb, who was the owner of a house, abandoned his house and gave it to the people who were supposed to be exchanged, and he was the one who moved in with his brother to the house adjacent to his own house. He left the house because he didn't want to be a man among the women, but he was the one who help them clean the house and all the hygiene requirements and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that clarifies the second question I had as well. So that is clear now. One other question is: They wanted to move to the other side of the confrontation line, those women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They wanted to either go home and it was left to us to exchange them one-for-one. But the main purpose of the police station in doing that was to learn about the lot of the 220 people, our own Serbs, that I mentioned, because nothing was known about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So these women, as a matter of fact, as you explain it, were dependent on whether there would be an exchange, whether the other party would agree to such an exchange. And if not, they couldn't go where they wanted to go; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Muslim side declined to agree to the exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And these women had to pay the price for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As far as I know, they were allowed to go back to Vlasenica, or rather, the driver, Radenko Zoranovic and another lad took them back to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand that they stayed for two months in a place waiting for the outcome of the -- the outcome of the talks for an exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not receive the interpretation of your question, or rather, I only received the interpretation of half of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will repeat it. I said: But I do understand that they stayed for two months in a place, and I meant that house, waiting for the outcome of the talks, the negotiations, for an exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you considered to just let them go to the other side, if that's what they wished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was later decided in consultations with Stanimir to take them back to Vlasenica because when our men saw that nothing would come out of all that, that's what they offered them as a solution and they agreed to go back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you offer them to go to the other side without an exchange just because they wished to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when our men learned that there would be no use of them, they told them that they could go either to the Kladanj or to Vlasenica and then they chose to go back to Vlasenica. Your Honour, I had three or four prisoners, and later they strung me along for months, and eventually what happened was that I made a decision and let them go. First we talked for two or three months and then they didn't want to exchange those soldiers for our men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These three or four prisoners you are talking about, who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were members of the BiH Army. One was taken prisoner in Kalesija, the other in Olovo, one in Zvornik. They are still alive and they work in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because you apparently make a comparison between a situation where six civilian females are waiting for the results of an exchange negotiation, and the other situation where you are talking about prisoners of war. Do you have any explanation as why you compare the two, which suggests that their situation is to some extent the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying is that the other side didn't want to talk to us. I also mention that I myself had three prisoners, soldiers of the BiH Army, and I offered to exchange them for just one member of the Serbian army and they declined that. So I was simply forced to let them go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can go back to D320, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pelemis, we shall go back to that document listing men involved in the march of your unit. After the operation, after the entry into Srebrenica, where were your men deployed? Who stayed? Who moved on?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which day?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 12th, when it ended.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime around 10.00 on the 12th, I received orders from the Drina Corps that my activities related to the resubordination to the Drina Corps shall stop at 1200 hours. Then I called the administration in Crna Rijeka, and the duty officer told me Salapura was absent and that he would inquire what to do next. A little bit later, he called me up and said that the unit should take furlough for a few days and then gather in Bijeljina in order to go to the area of the Herzegovina Corps in Kalesija. When we were in Srebrenica, we lined up next to the warehouse of the Red Cross, and I told my men, "Now we are going along the axis Srebrenica-Zeleni Jadar-Milici, et cetera. We shall lay down our equipment and you are all free to go until the 12th of July when we all need to assemble in the barracks."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be told to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you should slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. What we have on the record is that you told them they were free until the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Go on, but please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. Go on, what? We could go on forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was just interrupting the witness to correct this date, when he was talking about the 22nd of July, when they had the task to assemble in the barracks. As of 12th, he has to continue, who was where. I asked who was where after the 12th. That was my initial question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see what your original question was. The question was: "Where were your men deployed? Who stayed? Who moved on?" And then you interrupted him. He was in the midst of answering that question, although you could have perhaps taken him back more quickly to who had stayed and who moved on rather than to let the witness explain exactly by what route, et cetera, et cetera. So if you could take control again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in view of the interruption, there was nothing wrong with saying, "please go on." But please give some more guidance to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelemis, tell us, do you know who went where after the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, all the men on this list, the 26 we see here, most of them had left on the evening of the 12th to Bijeljina, to Vlasenica. They went on furlough. When Dragan Todorovic tried to organise the funeral and the departure for Trebinje, a little later he found three or four or five men who were available to go to the funeral. And the four or five men who stayed were sent to the villages around Srebrenica to collect food and equipment for the house. That's what I was told. Why, for instance, the 16th? On the 16th only this crew was there. They had come back from the funeral or they had returned from their trips to villages where they collected food. But 80 per cent of the men did take furlough as they had been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 16th, the men who went to Branjevo, did they go -- did they belong to one squad? How did they come to form this group?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking from here, Franc Kos, 1st Platoon, 1st Squad; Brano Gojkovic, 2nd Squad, 1st Platoon; Drazen Erdemovic, 1st Squad of the 1st Platoon; Goronja, 2nd Squad of the 2nd Platoon; Stanko Savanovic, he was from the 3rd Squad of the 2nd Platoon; Vlastimir Golijan, 1st Squad, 1st Platoon. So they were gathered from different groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can see it's the break time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How much time would you still need, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think I should finish in the next 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15. Mr. McCloskey, not knowing what the 15 minutes will be about, but as far as you can estimate now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one very short clarification on something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think we should not yet release the next witness. We should start with the next witness after the conclusion of this testimony. We'll take a break, Witness. You may follow the usher and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can have on our screens P1673, please. It's a statement by -- actually, yeah, testimony of Drazen Erdemovic in Rule 61 proceeding. I'll need to start from page 9, line 20, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask you something about your knowledge as to the allegations of Drazen Erdemovic. From line 20. I will read in English, so you will get the correct interpretation. [In English] "Q. Mr. Erdemovic, I now would like to turn your attention to 16th of July and ask you whether on that day you and other soldiers in your unit received orders to participate in a special detail?" And there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need next page, line 10, because there was some discussion in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question continues at line 1: "Did you receive orders at all that day from anybody in relation to a task or a mission that ultimately you went on? "A. Yes. "Q. From whom did you receive that orders? "A. From the group commander, Brano Gojkovic." Line 7: "Q. Did he normally give your unit orders to perform certain missions or was this an exception? "A. Yes, it was an exception." [Interpretation] Mr. Pelemis, let me ask you this: According to you in the group that included Franc Kos and Drazen Erdemovic, to the best of your knowledge, could that group be commanded by Brano Gojkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, who should be in command of that group which included Franc Kos and Drazen Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with our hierarchy, Franc Kos was in charge of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now see further on, from line 18 onwards. The question goes: [In English] "Q. In response to the orders" -- I quote: "In response to the orders that you received on 16 July, Mr. Erdemovic, where did you go next? "A. We went to Zvornik, and Brano Gojkovic and the driver reported to a lieutenant-colonel whose name I do not know."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we'll have to go to the next page. Line 9 and further. "Q. After there were some conversations between Brano and lieutenant-colonel, what happened next? "A. They told us to sit in the car and to accompany the vehicle with the lieutenant-colonel and the two military policemen. We went from Zvornik in the direction of Bijeljina, and on the road we stopped at a farm that was at a place called Pilica." Then we need the next page, line 10, please. The end of the -- that row, it starts "After ..." so it's: "Q. After you arrived at that farm, Mr. Erdemovic, did you receive additional orders from your superiors? "A. I personally did not, but I heard when Brano and the lieutenant-colonel were talking, saying that buses would be coming to the farm. "Q. In relation to those buses, did you receive any additional information? "A. Afterwards when the lieutenant-colonel left, Brano said that buses would be coming with Muslims from Srebrenica. "Q. Did he say what you and the members of your unit were supposed to do regarding those Muslims from Srebrenica? "A. Yes. "Q. What did he say? "A. That we have to execute those people, to shoot them. "Q. When you say 'he' told you you had to shoot them, for the record, who was that, if you could identify him by name? "A. Brano Gojkovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pelemis, from what you know, who gave the orders to move, who approved the issuing of equipment, and who was the commander of the group when receiving orders in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a three-part question. And also the foundation. You know from what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you lay a foundation for the knowledge of the witness, and that may perhaps be different for the various questions, and split them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've told us that Brano Gojkovic, in your view, could not command that group that included Franc Kos and Drazen Erdemovic. You've told us that, in your opinion, that group could only be commanded by Franc Kos. Do you know who issued the order for that group to move, that group that was made up of different squads of your detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Dragan Todorovic, the logistics man of the 10th Sabotage Detachment who was in the unit on the 16th, I learned that the vehicle and the equipment normally issued to one squad was taken over by Second-Lieutenant Franc Kos and that their assignment was to go to the command of the Zvornik Brigade to receive further orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just understand what the equipment was, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The standard equipment for one infantry squad: A case of ammunition, one machine-gun, and eight automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have -- we tried yesterday to see something on the video P1147, and it was video. I'll try to replace it by one still from that video. It's 1D5380. So if we can have that one on our screens, please. Can we enlarge just the picture, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, as we were watching the video, you told us that you saw that the man had been wounded in the back. Although the quality of the video is not perfect, would you say that the blood-stain is visible on this man's back?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by my assertion that the man was wounded in the back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether that was on the basis of you identifying a blood-stain on the back of that person as is shown to us now in the photograph. That was the question. Not whether you still think that he was shot in the back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe that he was hit in the back, and I base that on the blood-stain or blood-stains on his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If he had been shot in the chest, would he still have wounds in the back?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those would be entry/exit wounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of course if you want to continue like this, use your time as you wish, but of course if I'm shot in the chest, whether there is a bullet-hole in my back, you couldn't tell. The bullet could have stopped, the bullet could have deviated. There are many, many, many possible explanations which usually are dealt with by experts who have carefully examined the body so therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- yesterday this witness said: I am not sure because -- this is what I conclude from the photo, and he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You ask him now if he had been shot in the chest, would he still have wounds in the back. There is no way that this witness could answer that question. If you would have asked him if you're shot in the chest, does that necessarily mean that there is no bullet-hole on the back? That's a different question, still for an expert, but I think that many who have often dealt with these kind of matters, even if not full experts, could come up with an answer as the witness gave us. But let's try to remain serious for ourselves. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Still, I would offer this photo into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a still from the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the same video, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the witness, before it goes into evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, I can tell you this still is made by the Prosecution, and it was introduced in Tolimir case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's in this case, too. It's in the still book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore most need to have it in evidence if that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But before it goes away from the screen, could the witness identify to us the blood-stain that is on the back and how we determine what is the back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the middle of the back ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, somebody has to help the witness with a pen. He pressed the screen and it was just blown up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness marked the photograph, and I take it that you want to tender that, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D979, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still from a video marked by the witness admitted into evidence. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I've just been informed, I was -- we were wrong about that. This was not -- it was in the Tolimir book, not in the Mladic book. So -- but we now have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have it now, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And the second part of Judge Moloto's question, how it is visible that this person is on -- lying on his stomach, it's much better visible from the video, and yesterday we saw it that he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are looking at this exhibit now. I am aware of that. I'm asking about this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, if you want to ask the witness so he can answer that part of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I did ask the question. Do you want me to repeat it, sir? How do you determine that this person is lying on his tummy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can see in the photo that he is on his stomach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see blood-stains in the middle of the back, which indicates that he was wounded in the back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're answering a different question. You did tell us that he's got blood-stains on the back. I'm asking you how do determine that that is his back. You can't say it's his back because it's got blood-stains.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, as I'm looking at this photo, I think that the man is lying on his stomach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's everything. Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I just have another topic and I'll hopefully finish soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it means that the next witness can be excused anyhow that's -- because we'll not start his testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague Ivetic will inform our case manager, so it will be done. Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have on our screens 1D5378, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier today, Mr. Pelemis, you mentioned a person called Stanimir Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see his statement here. He gave it to the CSB Zvornik. He spoke about attacks against Pelemisi village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no English translation. We need next page from this statement, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then first identify with the witness what it is, what we're looking at at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you -- sorry. Can we go back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first see whether the witness has -- have you seen this document before, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please introduce the document, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a statement provided on the 11th of July, 1994, by Stanimir Pelemis, son of Stevan, mother's name Danica. He talks about war crimes, the war crimes that happened in Jelacici and Pelemisi and he provides a statement. Earlier today you told us that the village had been attacked five times or, rather, that it had fallen five times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who answered this "yes"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see a list of names here. It says the first attack on the Serbian village of Pelemisi happened on the Easter of 1993. The village was set on fire. All the 35 households were set on fire. The second time the village was attacked was in March 1994. On that occasion, the following persons were killed. What follows is a list of ten names. The third time the Serbian village of Pelemisi was attacked was on the 20th of April, 1994, on Easter, from the direction of Stanova and from the direction of Kladanj. Among the persons whose names you see here, did you know anybody personally?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Milos Pepic, under number 1. Nenad Vidovic, under 2. Miroljub, under number 5. I personally knew persons under number 1 and 2 and 4 in the second batch.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell us their names.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Pepic from Pepici, who was my neighbour, his head was cut off. We found the head some 200 metres away from the body. Nenad Vidovic was a PE teacher, retired. Miroljub Milicic was from Popovici. He was a forest worker. Ljubisa Radojcic from Sekovici was a driver. These are the people who I can remember as I sit here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to your 10th Sabotage Detachment, were there any members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment who participated in the attacks against Pelemisi?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, 1993, Zijad Zigic and Franc Kos participated in the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As members of what units at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assault units of the 2nd Tuzla Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of what army?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact when they joined your unit, the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they admitted that to me as soon as I joined the 10th Sabotage Detachment. I never held it against them. I did not hate them. I really tried to help them as much as I could when they were in my unit. I am still friends with Zijad Zigic. And let me just tell you that on that occasion they killed a 70 -- or Stojan Vucinovic, who was my kum. They set him on fire. And to this very day, we have not managed to put two bones in his body together. They set him in fire in a haystack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am just wondering how this arises from cross-examination. I notice that the witness sometimes, not solicited to do that, gave some information on matters not asked to him which deal with it. I also noticed that at least the statement, paragraph 5, deals with this matter. So therefore it could have been easily elicited in examination-in-chief. I let it go for a while, but I take it, Mr. Lukic, that you'll move on soon and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just have one more question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelemis, could you just tell us how many members of your family were killed during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: 11, both on my wife's side and my own side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pelemis. This is all we had for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity for further questions by the Prosecution. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pelemis, what could you tell us about the suspicions that were raised and what activity is ongoing in the courts of Bosnia and Herzegovina against you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. If I get invited by the court, I am fully prepared to go there to prove my innocence. I personally never killed a man nor did I ever order anybody else to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're willing to go there if they would like to ask questions to you? Or if they want to treat you as a suspect, you're willing to go and to defend yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Certainly, yes. I know that I am innocent and I am perfectly willing to prove my innocence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if there is a warrant of arrest against you, why would you then not go?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will talk to the lawyers about that, and I will consult with them to see what I'm supposed to do. In legal terms, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you told us that you were willing to go. You don't need a lawyer to say, "I want to go." Apparently you're not at this moment yet ready to go, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- it's not true that he does not need a lawyer to decide whether to go or not. I would not agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic, I am not in a debate with you. Every suspect or accused --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- can make up his mind himself whether he wants to go or not. And if he wants to see a lawyer to find out, of course you can do that. But to make up your mind as to whether to go, I asked the witness, "Are you willing to go?" You said, "Yes." And then I said, "Why don't you go," and then you said, "I have to see a lawyer." So your willingness is conditional. And that's exactly the reason, Mr. Lukic, why I consider your intervention inappropriate. So your willingness is conditional.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This will be my first time before a court. I don't know what I'm supposed to do. I don't know what charges I'm supposed to fight, whether they are false charges. This will not be a 50 euro damages case. I need a lawyer because I may be facing some false accusations, something that will have a huge impact on my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, "I want to go there and prove my innocence." That's usually against false accusations, isn't it? Otherwise, there is no need -- if you're innocent, then there is no need to prove your -- to prove that innocence. I mean, you'd told us you would go there and prove your innocence. Of course, you only have to prove your innocence, apart from whether you have to do that in a court, if someone accuses you falsely. Otherwise, there is no evidence and there is no need to prove any innocence.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what I did. I know that there is nothing I should fear. I am afraid of false statements, false witnesses, of the things that happen in Sarajevo. I can't be certain about any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is why, until now, you are not willing to go there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- to be able to lead this discussion, we have to know domestic laws. There is agreement in between Bosnia and Serbia. He's there, he's in Serbia. According to that agreement, whether he was in Bosnia or in Serbia, he's there. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- he can be summoned any time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the only thing I know is that the Defence brought to our attention a statement in which the witness clearly expresses his concerns as having to appear before a court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, isn't it? And I leave it to that. If you want at any point in time for purposes of credibility of this witness put anything to our attention, you have an opportunity to do so but not in the context of my questioning of the witness on this matter. That's as simple as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a citizen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a citizen of Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- he cannot be tried in Bosnia. He has to be tried in Serbia according to that agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, again, if there is no problem, if he only can be tried in Serbia, because that's what you're telling us --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- why would you worry about --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- he cannot be extradited from Serbia to Bosnia. There is agreement between those two states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, I'm stopping this, Mr. Lukic. If at any other point in time you want to pursue this matter, you can do that, but not as part of the examination of this witness, this witness who told us that he is willing to appear before the court which brings charges against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because he's not legally educated. He does not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, let's stop it. Any further questions, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This should hopefully be very brief. Further Cross-examination by McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said on page 56, in talking about Erdemovic -- actually, it's at page 57, line 1: "He signed a contract with the Ministry of Defence, i.e., the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska, and that's where he was given his rank and then he was promoted, as we see in the video-clip, that he became the second-lieutenant." Did you say that, that we saw from the video-clip he had become a second-lieutenant or was it some other rank?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said staff sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. So that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is just a -- an important miscue for the record. We'll get that sorted out. It's a mistranslation, actually. And I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pelemis, this concludes your evidence in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic and Mr. McCloskey, if any of you think that the answers of the witness in relation to whether he has to fear anything from being prosecuted wherever, if any documentation - be it legislation, be it information about the case - apparently initiated by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Chamber, of course if there's any need for you, will look at those materials if you think that it would clarify answers the witness has given specifically about his willingness to appear before a court where he is indicted or at least where an arrest warrant was issued against him. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I -- as you will recall, I guess it was Thursday and the witness had stated he had given a statement to the office of the prosecutor in the state court. We have been in touch with the state court to see what we could get, if anything. I do have some information. I actually just received it this morning. And given your -- what you've just requested, I -- it appears to be -- and I don't know, because I haven't had even a chance to really understand what it is, but a letter from a lawyer that may be -- may have represented this man back in 2010, and it appears to be some sort of statement in what we believe in his handwriting. So it appears as if a lawyer sent a -- some sort of statement from this witness and -- to the state court in Bosnia. Because I am just not sure what it is, I did not engage the witness with it. But given your specific question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it would be appropriate to first share that information with Mr. Lukic. And if there is any further reason to bring this to the attention of the Court, parties have an opportunity to do so, especially in relation to my questions which were directly related to his willingness, I think, as he said, to prove his innocence, and that's usually what you do before a court. I leave it to that for the time being. My apologies to all those assisting. You have an opportunity to consult after we have adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We -- yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was that one issue that you had delayed for the witness. I don't know if you want to do it now. It was a dead-line you had set for the Defence to respond on some things today. I can do it via e-mail if that's easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that's easier --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and it would not be a further burden on those who are assisting us at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We went already far beyond the time I should have gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I just make -- just so your words don't get twisted in the future. You've just made a comment that one may -- "I think, as he said, to prove his innocence, and that's usually what you do before a court," and I know what you meant, that that was an opportunity for a person that may choose to prove his innocence, but it shouldn't be ever twisted to mean a person has a burden to prove their innocence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think I emphasized that already earlier. But some people who are charged before a court take the position that they'll defend themselves by proving their innocence, whereas it goes without saying that that's not what you have to do. But of course, you are not forbidden to do that. But even if you have not proven your innocence and if the prosecution has not proven your guilt, then you still should be acquitted despite the fact that you have not proven your innocence because that's not required for an acquittal. Is this understood by everyone sufficiently so as to avoid any confusion for the future?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I appreciate that. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, the 31st of March, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
